title: Levers & biomechanics
examples: Can you show me an example of a first-class lever?
What is the difference between the effort and the load?
How do the planes of motion affect levers?

explain.say: Today we will explore levers and how they work in the human body. You will learn about three main types of levers. We will also look at the planes of movement.
Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: a lever. Look at the fulcrum, the load and the effort. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.
A first-class lever has the load and effort on opposite sides of the fulcrum. Think about a seesaw balancing two people. The fulcrum is right in the middle.
A second-class lever has the load between the fulcrum and the effort. A wheelbarrow is a perfect example of this type of machine.
In a third-class lever, the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load. Your forearm when you bend it is a common example.
The planes of movement help us describe body actions accurately. The sagittal plane divides the body into left and right halves. Think about jumping forward.
When you swing your arm forward, you are moving in the frontal plane. This plane moves the body side to side, like a side-to-side motion.

draw.text: Frontal Plane: Side to Side Motion

faq.q: What is the difference between the planes of movement?
faq.a: The planes describe the imaginary slices through the body. The sagittal plane splits you into left and right halves. You might also ask about the frontal or transverse plane.
asks: What are the planes of motion?

faq.q: Which class of lever is the human forearm?
faq.a: The human forearm acts as a third-class lever. The effort is applied by your muscles between the joint and the load. You could also ask about the elbow joint or muscle action.
asks: Is the arm a first or third class lever?
Where is the effort on the forearm?
What kind of lever is the elbow?

faq.q: Does the size of the load change the lever class?
faq.a: No, the class of the lever depends on the order of the three points. The relationship between the fulcrum, load, and effort determines the class. You might also ask if weight matters.
asks: Does the resistance change the lever type?
Is it always the same class?
Does the load size matter for the class?

faq.q: What is the fulcrum in a lever system?
faq.a: The fulcrum is the fixed point or pivot around which the lever moves. It is the point of support, like the middle of a seesaw. You can also ask what the pivot point is.
asks: What is the center of rotation?

faq.q: What is the effort in biomechanics?
faq.a: Effort is the force you apply to move the load. It is the force generated by the muscles. You might also ask what the applied force is.
asks: Where do I apply the force?

facts: A first-class lever has the fulcrum between the effort and the load.
The wheelbarrow demonstrates a second-class lever arrangement.
The forearm is a common example of a third-class lever.
The sagittal plane divides the body into left and right halves.

quiz.say: A seesaw where the two people sit are the load and effort. The middle point is the fulcrum. What class of lever is this?
quiz.why: The fulcrum is in the middle, separating the load and effort, which defines a first-class lever.

wrong.1: This is wrong because the load is not positioned between the fulcrum and the effort.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the effort is not applied between the fulcrum and the load.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the arrangement perfectly matches the definition of a first-class lever.

quiz.say: A person standing on a wheelbarrow pushing up on the handles. What type of lever is this?
quiz.why: The load is between the fulcrum and the effort, which correctly identifies a second-class lever.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the wheelbarrow uses mechanical principles of levers.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the load is not on the opposite side of the fulcrum from the effort.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the effort is not applied between the fulcrum and the load.

quiz.say: When moving your wrist up against gravity, which plane of motion are you primarily using?
quiz.why: Movement up and down, like flexing the wrist, occurs in the sagittal plane, dividing the body into left and right.

wrong.1: This is wrong because the frontal plane involves side-to-side movement, like abduction.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the transverse plane involves rotation, not simple up and down movement.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the motion described is a clear example of sagittal plane action.
